newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOYBEANS - Brazil state awaits end of wheat crop.
newsitem.headline: SOYBEANS - Brazil state awaits end of wheat crop.

text.p: Planting in one of Brazil's top two producing states, Parana, is expected only to really get going by mid-November due to a rain-induced delay in bringing in the wheat harvest, a state agronomist said.

"The wheat harvest is still going very slowly. The rain is slowing everything down and I think we will only be finished by the middle of November," said Otmar Hubner of the Parana State Agricultural Secretariat.

By October 12, 63 percent of the wheat harvest had been brought in against an historical average of 80 percent. Heavy rains over the past week had not helped improve the situation and were leading to losses in the harvest, Hubner said.
The south and the southeast of the state were worst hit, with some soybean plantings taking place in other areas.
But while 15 percent of soybean plantings are normally completed by the end this month, so far only 0.5 percent of this year's anticipated crop was in the ground, Hubner said.

The secretariat is expecting planted area to total 2.48 million hectares, up from last year's 2.3 million, while production should range between 6.25 million and 6.7 million tonnes against 6.38 million in 1995/96.
For the time being, the delay did not represent any cause for concern, with plantings perfectly viable until the end of the year, Hubner said.

Farmers in Rio Grande do Sul, traditionally Brazil's largest soybean producing state, will meanwhile start sowing the crop this week, said Valdir Bisotto of Fecotrigo, the state cooperatives' federation.
The recent rains if anything have been advantageous as they helped prepare the grounds for planting.
"The ideal is that we have rains every 10 days to help germination," Bisotto said.
Temperatures however were a little on the low side at just under 20 degrees Celsius compared to a preferred 20 to 25 degrees Celsius, he added.

Planted area is expected to exceed last year's 2.76 million hectares and should hopefully return to the three million hectares or so seen in 1994/95, with production forecast to pass six million tonnes.
Brazilian soybean production in 1996/97 should reach 25.89 million tonnes based on current planting intentions, said independent consultants Safras e Mercado.

Around 15 percent of this has already been committed, up from seven percent at the same stage last year and an historical average of 12 percent, stimulated by the higher prices seen in the markets through most of this year, Safras said today.
However the recent fall in world prices has put new sales on hold for the time being, said analyst Falvio Franca.
-- Caroline Bulloch, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
